fragment_text: This learning page introduces software design, programming paradigms, performance considerations, testing, deployment, and responding to user requirements. Software development begins with understanding the needs of users and translating those needs into clear software requirements. During software design, developers define the architecture, components, interfaces, data structures, and interactions required by the system. Different programming paradigms, such as object-oriented, procedural, functional, and event-driven programming, may be selected depending on the problem. Developers must also consider software performance. This includes execution speed, memory consumption, scalability, response time, and efficient use of computing resources. Testing and verification are performed before deployment to identify defects and confirm that the software satisfies its requirements.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["Different programming paradigms, such as object-oriented, procedural, functional, and event-driven programming, may be selected depending on the problem.", "Testing and verification are performed before deployment to identify defects and confirm that the software satisfies its requirements."]
short_reasoning: The paragraph teaches software requirements, design, programming paradigms, performance, and deployment (GI_C1_1). A separate sentence independently teaches testing and verification against requirements (GI_C1_2).

fragment_text: Deployment is the process of preparing and releasing the software into a production environment. It may include configuration, packaging, installation, monitoring, maintenance, and future updates. A successful software product therefore combines user requirements, software design, programming paradigms, performance evaluation, testing, deployment, and maintenance.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["Deployment is the process of preparing and releasing the software into a production environment."]
short_reasoning: The fragment explains deployment, packaging, installation, and maintenance as part of delivering software. That is the child competency for software development and production release, not a separate quality-engineering lesson.

fragment_text: This page explains user-centered design, interface prototyping, usability, accessibility, ergonomics, mobile interfaces, and user experience evaluation. Human-computer interaction focuses on how people communicate with software systems and digital devices. User-centered design begins by identifying the users, their goals, their tasks, and the context in which the system will be used. Designers collect user requirements through interviews, observation, questionnaires, and usability studies. A prototype is an early representation of an interface. It may be a paper sketch, wireframe, interactive mock-up, or functional prototype. Prototypes allow designers to test ideas before completing the final implementation. User experience includes usefulness, ease of use, efficiency, satisfaction, clarity, and trust.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["This page explains user-centered design, interface prototyping, usability, accessibility, ergonomics, mobile interfaces, and user experience evaluation."]
short_reasoning: The paragraph is a direct HCI/UX lesson: users, tasks, context, prototyping, and user-experience criteria. GI_C1_3 is the matching child competency.

fragment_text: A good interface should provide clear navigation, consistent controls, readable content, useful feedback, and understandable error messages. Accessibility ensures that people with different abilities can use the system. Examples include keyboard navigation, sufficient colour contrast, alternative text for images, captions for multimedia, readable typography, and compatibility with assistive technologies. Ergonomics considers the physical and cognitive comfort of users. Mobile, virtual-reality, and augmented-reality interfaces also require careful attention to screen size, interaction methods, orientation, movement, safety, and user fatigue. Usability testing evaluates whether representative users can complete important tasks accurately, efficiently, and comfortably.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["Mobile, virtual-reality, and augmented-reality interfaces also require careful attention to screen size, interaction methods, orientation, movement, safety, and user fatigue."]
short_reasoning: Accessibility, ergonomics, usability testing, and mobile/VR/AR interaction are the HCI/UX child competency, not general software construction.

fragment_text: This page introduces distributed systems, concurrency, communication between services, scalability, fault tolerance, performance, and security. A distributed system is a collection of independent computers or software services that communicate through a network and work together as one system. Distributed applications divide processing, storage, and services across several machines. Common examples include cloud applications, web services, online banking platforms, content-delivery networks, and large e-commerce systems. Concurrency occurs when several tasks execute during overlapping periods. Concurrent programs must coordinate access to shared resources to avoid race conditions, inconsistent data, deadlocks, and unexpected behaviour. Communication between distributed components may use message queues, remote procedure calls, web APIs, events, or service-oriented architecture.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["A distributed system is a collection of independent computers or software services that communicate through a network and work together as one system."]
short_reasoning: The fragment teaches distributed applications, concurrency, and service communication (queues, RPC, web APIs, SOA). That is distributed software and scalability, not a hardware-network architecture lesson.

fragment_text: Each component should define clear interfaces and handle communication failures correctly. Scalability is the ability of a system to continue operating efficiently as the number of users, requests, or stored records increases. Vertical scaling adds more resources to one machine, while horizontal scaling distributes the workload across additional machines. Load balancing distributes requests between several servers. Caching reduces repeated computation and database access. Database replication and partitioning can also improve availability and performance. Distributed systems must tolerate partial failures. One server or network connection may fail while other parts of the system continue working. Monitoring, retries, timeouts, redundancy, and fault-recovery mechanisms are therefore important. Security must be considered across all components.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["Scalability is the ability of a system to continue operating efficiently as the number of users, requests, or stored records increases."]
short_reasoning: Horizontal/vertical scaling, load balancing, caching, replication, and partial-failure handling are the scalability side of distributed software.

fragment_text: Authentication, authorization, encryption, secure communication, logging, and protection against malicious requests help reduce distributed-system risks. A successful distributed system balances concurrency, scalability, performance, availability, fault tolerance, consistency, and security.
suggested_ambiguity_reason: The paragraph teaches security controls, but it is the closing wrap-up of a distributed-systems page, so both cybersecurity and distributed-software readings are defensible.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["Authentication, authorization, encryption, secure communication, logging, and protection against malicious requests help reduce distributed-system risks.", "A successful distributed system balances concurrency, scalability, performance, availability, fault tolerance, consistency, and security."]
short_reasoning: The first sentence is a cybersecurity controls lesson (GI_C2_3). The second sentence restates the whole distributed-system trade-off set (GI_C1_4). Both are independently present.

fragment_text: This page introduces software and hardware architectures, operating systems, networked systems, cloud and IoT architectures, cybersecurity, cryptography, risk analysis, and resilience. Computer architecture describes how hardware and software components are organized to execute programs and provide computing services. Hardware architecture includes processors, memory, storage devices, buses, sensors, actuators, and input-output components. Software architecture defines operating systems, services, interfaces, modules, and communication between software components. Operating systems manage hardware resources, processes, memory, files, devices, and user access. Architects must consider performance, reliability, energy consumption, resource limitations, and maintainability. Networked architectures allow computers and services to communicate.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["Hardware architecture includes processors, memory, storage devices, buses, sensors, actuators, and input-output components."]
short_reasoning: The paragraph explains how hardware and software components, operating systems, energy, and resource limits are organized. That is GI_C2_1 rather than a networking or security child.

fragment_text: Local networks, wide-area networks, cloud platforms, fog computing, and Internet of Things systems connect devices and distribute processing across several locations. Cloud computing provides shared computing resources, storage, databases, and applications over a network. Fog and edge computing move part of the processing closer to sensors and users to reduce delay and network traffic. Cybersecurity protects systems, networks, applications, and data against unauthorized access, disruption, modification, and destruction. Risk analysis identifies valuable assets, possible threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood, and potential impact. Security controls are then selected to reduce these risks. Cryptography protects information using techniques such as encryption, hashing, digital signatures, and secure key management.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["Local networks, wide-area networks, cloud platforms, fog computing, and Internet of Things systems connect devices and distribute processing across several locations.", "Cybersecurity protects systems, networks, applications, and data against unauthorized access, disruption, modification, and destruction."]
short_reasoning: The first half independently teaches communicating architectures (networks, cloud, fog, IoT). The second half independently teaches risk analysis, cybersecurity, and cryptography.

fragment_text: Authentication verifies identity, while authorization controls what an authenticated user may access. Secure architectures also require intrusion detection, monitoring, logging, software updates, backup systems, access control, network segmentation, and incident-response procedures. Resilience is the ability of a system to continue operating or recover quickly after failures or cyberattacks. A secure architecture must therefore combine prevention, detection, response, recovery, performance, and availability.

short_reasoning: Authentication, authorization, intrusion detection, and cyber-resilience are the safe-architecture / cybersecurity child competency.

fragment_text: This page introduces knowledge representation, formal logic, ontologies, semantic relationships, automated reasoning, ethics, bias, and regulatory considerations. Knowledge representation is the process of describing information in a structured form that a computer system can store, interpret, and use for reasoning. Formal logic provides rules for representing statements and determining whether conclusions follow from known facts. Propositional logic uses statements that are either true or false, while predicate logic represents objects, properties, variables, and relationships. An ontology defines the concepts of a domain and the relationships between those concepts. It may contain classes, properties, individuals, constraints, and hierarchical relationships such as parent and child concepts.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["An ontology defines the concepts of a domain and the relationships between those concepts."]
short_reasoning: Knowledge representation, formal logic, and ontologies are the KR/reasoning child competency.

fragment_text: For example, an educational ontology may represent courses, learning resources, competencies, teachers, students, and assessment activities. It can also describe relationships such as a learning resource teaches a competency or a quiz evaluates a competency. The Semantic Web uses structured data and shared vocabularies so that computers can interpret relationships between information from different sources. Automated reasoning applies logical rules to existing knowledge to derive new conclusions. A reasoning system may detect inconsistencies, infer missing relationships, classify concepts, or verify whether conditions are satisfied. Knowledge-based systems must also consider uncertainty, incomplete information, conflicting evidence, and the reliability of data sources.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["The Semantic Web uses structured data and shared vocabularies so that computers can interpret relationships between information from different sources."]
short_reasoning: Ontological relationships, Semantic Web vocabularies, and automated reasoning remain GI_C3_1.

fragment_text: Ethical issues include privacy, transparency, explainability, discrimination, and the possibility of biased knowledge structures. Regulations may require systems to protect personal information and explain important automated decisions. A well-designed knowledge representation system combines clear concepts, meaningful relationships, logical consistency, traceable evidence, ethical safeguards, and appropriate regulatory controls.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["Ethical issues include privacy, transparency, explainability, discrimination, and the possibility of biased knowledge structures."]

fragment_text: This page introduces relational database design, tables, keys, normalization, transactions, NoSQL databases, document stores, key-value databases, scalability, security, and data consistency. A database is an organized collection of data that can be stored, updated, searched, and managed by a computer system. Relational databases represent information using tables. Each table contains rows and columns. A row represents one record, while a column represents an attribute of that record. A primary key uniquely identifies each row. A foreign key creates a relationship between records stored in different tables. These keys help preserve data integrity and connect related information. Database design normally begins with identifying entities, attributes, and relationships. An entity may represent a student, course, teacher, product, or order.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["Relational databases represent information using tables."]
short_reasoning: Tables, keys, entities, and relational design are the data/databases child competency.

fragment_text: Relationships describe how these entities are connected. Normalization organizes relational tables to reduce duplication and update problems. It separates data into related tables while preserving meaningful connections between records. Transactions group several database operations into one logical unit. Reliable transactions follow the ACID principles: atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability. Relational database systems commonly use SQL for defining tables, inserting data, updating records, deleting records, and retrieving information. NoSQL databases use models other than traditional relational tables. Common types include document databases, key-value stores, column-oriented databases, and graph databases. Document databases store flexible structured documents, often using JSON-like formats.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["NoSQL databases use models other than traditional relational tables."]
short_reasoning: Normalization, ACID transactions, SQL, and NoSQL models are still database modelling and storage (GI_C3_2).

fragment_text: Key-value databases associate unique keys with stored values and are useful for fast lookups and caching. NoSQL systems may be suitable for large-scale applications, rapidly changing data structures, distributed storage, or workloads that require flexible schemas. Database designers must consider consistency, availability, scalability, security, backup, recovery, indexing, query performance, and access control. The choice between relational and NoSQL databases depends on the structure of the data, application requirements, expected workload, consistency needs, and scaling strategy.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["The choice between relational and NoSQL databases depends on the structure of the data, application requirements, expected workload, consistency needs, and scaling strategy."]
short_reasoning: Key-value/document stores and the relational vs NoSQL design choice belong to GI_C3_2.

fragment_text: This page explains SQL selection, filtering, joins, grouping, aggregation, subqueries, views, indexes, data analysis, and the use of database information to support decisions. Structured Query Language, or SQL, is used to define, retrieve, modify, and manage data in relational database systems. A SELECT query retrieves data from one or more tables. The WHERE clause filters rows according to specific conditions, while ORDER BY sorts the result. For example, a query may retrieve all students enrolled in a course, all orders created during a specific month, or all products with a price above a selected value. Joins combine related information from multiple tables. An INNER JOIN returns matching records from both tables. LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN operations can also preserve unmatched records from one side of the relationship. Aggregation functions summarize groups of records.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["A SELECT query retrieves data from one or more tables."]
short_reasoning: SQL selection, filtering, and joins are querying relational data for decision support (GI_C3_2).

fragment_text: Common functions include COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX. The GROUP BY clause creates groups based on one or more columns. The HAVING clause filters aggregated groups after calculations have been performed. Subqueries place one query inside another query. They may be used to compare a value with an aggregate result, identify records that satisfy several conditions, or build intermediate result sets. Database views store reusable query definitions. A view may simplify a complex query, restrict access to sensitive fields, or present information in a convenient format. Indexes improve retrieval performance by creating efficient access paths to data. However, indexes also require storage and can increase the cost of insert and update operations. Decision-support systems transform stored data into information that helps users evaluate situations and choose actions.
suggested_exact_evidence: ["Decision-support systems transform stored data into information that helps users evaluate situations and choose actions."]
short_reasoning: GROUP BY, HAVING, views, indexes, and decision-support queries remain GI_C3_2 rather than machine learning.

fragment_text: Examples include sales summaries, student-performance dashboards, inventory reports, risk indicators, financial analysis, and operational monitoring. Useful decision support requires accurate data, appropriate queries, meaningful indicators, understandable visualizations, and awareness of uncertainty or missing information. SQL therefore supports both routine database operations and analytical tasks involving filtering, relationships, aggregation, comparison, reporting, and evidence-based decision-making.

Classification predicts categories such as spam or legitimate email, positive or negative sentiment, or high-risk and low-risk cases. Regression predicts numerical values such as price, demand, or processing time. A model must be evaluated using data that was not used during training. Common classification measures include accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and the confusion matrix. Natural language processing enables computers to work with human language. Common NLP tasks include text classification, information extraction, summarization, question answering, translation, and sentiment analysis.
